extracted.intended_audience: undergraduate mathematics students learning proof techniques (discrete/introductory proofs)
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance and standards for composing and structuring elementary mathematical proofs, with emphasis on proof by contradiction, contrapositive, direct proof, existence/uniqueness, and if-and-only-if/equivalence proofs. Intended for students learning how to produce logically correct, well-signposted proofs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Proof by contradiction outline
rubrics_metrics.description: To prove a statement P: 'Suppose ~P. Therefore C ∧ ~C.' Conclude P is true.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Outline given explicitly: begin with the assumption that ~P is true, deduce an obvious contradiction C ∧ ¬C, then conclude P. The text shows this is logically valid via a truth table and equivalence of P with (~P) ⇒ (C ∧ ¬C).

rubrics_metrics.name: Contradiction (definition and role)
rubrics_metrics.description: A statement of the form C ∧ ¬C is called a contradiction; it cannot be true.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Contradictions are used as the target conclusion when assuming the negation of the desired statement; any statement that is clearly false will suffice as the contradiction (not necessarily of the form C ∧ ¬C). Examples: '1 is even' or nonsensical equalities.

rubrics_metrics.name: Signpost that you are using contradiction
rubrics_metrics.description: It is helpful (though not mandatory) to tip the reader off that you are using proof by contradiction, e.g. begin with 'Suppose for the sake of contradiction that ...'.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This signposting clarifies proof strategy for the reader; using the phrase 'for the sake of contradiction' is recommended.

rubrics_metrics.name: Negation of implication rule (how to set up conditional contradiction)
rubrics_metrics.description: To prove 'If P, then Q' by contradiction, start by assuming P and ¬Q, because ¬(P ⇒ Q) is equivalent to P ∧ ¬Q.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Outline provided: 'Proposition If P, then Q. Proof. Suppose P and ¬Q. Therefore C ∧ ¬C.' Use this when proving conditional statements with contradiction.

rubrics_metrics.name: Logical equivalence justification
rubrics_metrics.description: Showing (~P) ⇒ (C ∧ ¬C) is logically equivalent to P (so proving (~P) ⇒ (C ∧ ¬C) proves P).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The textbook demonstrates this with a truth table illustrating that columns for P and (~P) ⇒ (C ∧ ¬C) are identical; use this as the formal justification for proof by contradiction.

rubrics_metrics.name: Discovery process in contradiction proofs
rubrics_metrics.description: You may not know the contradiction C at the beginning; assume ¬P and deduce new statements until you obtain some C and ¬C.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Perform scratch work under the assumption ¬P to derive useful consequences; the contradiction may emerge only after several steps.

rubrics_metrics.name: When contradiction often works well (use cases)
rubrics_metrics.description: Proof by contradiction often works well for statements of the form ∀x P(x) because ¬∀x P(x) is equivalent to ∃x ¬P(x), which gives a specific x to work with.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: irrationality proofs where assuming ¬(∀x P(x)) yields an explicit counterexample instance to drive the contradiction.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prefer direct or contrapositive if simpler
rubrics_metrics.description: Although powerful, use proof by contradiction only when direct and contrapositive approaches do not seem to work, because a contradiction proof may hide a simpler contrapositive proof.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Authors illustrate an example where the contradiction proof essentially performs the contrapositive; choose the simpler, clearer method when available.

rubrics_metrics.name: Procedure for if-and-only-if proofs
rubrics_metrics.description: To prove 'P if and only if Q', prove both 'If P then Q' and 'If Q then P' (each may use direct, contrapositive, or contradiction).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Outline: perform the two proofs separately; begin the second part with a new paragraph and (preferably) the word 'Conversely' to signal the shift to the converse direction.

rubrics_metrics.name: Signposting converses
rubrics_metrics.description: When proving the converse (Q ⇒ P), begin the paragraph with 'Conversely' and remind the reader exactly what statement that paragraph is proving.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This structural advice improves readability and clarity when doing biconditional proofs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Proving equivalent statements via implication cycles
rubrics_metrics.description: To prove a list of statements are all equivalent, prove a set of conditional implications that form a cycle so each statement implies another and the cycle closes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A circular chain of n implications yields the fewest conditionals to prove equivalence; other non-circular schemes also work. Each conditional may use any proof technique.

rubrics_metrics.name: Existence proof method (constructive existence)
rubrics_metrics.description: To prove an existential statement ∃x R(x), provide and display a specific example x for which R(x) is true.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Often simple: produce the example and, if needed, verify the claimed property holds; examples given include '2 is an even prime' or the taxicab number 1729 for sums of cubes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Warning: example suffices for existence but not for conditional
rubrics_metrics.description: Although an example suffices to prove an existence statement, a single example does not prove a conditional or universally quantified statement.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be careful not to confuse existence proofs with proofs of general statements; the latter require argument for all cases, not a single exemplar.

rubrics_metrics.name: Proving existence inside conditionals (∀x ∃y ...)
rubrics_metrics.description: When an existence statement is embedded inside a conditional (e.g. ∀x P(x) ⇒ ∃y R(x,y)), assume the hypothesis and then produce the required example (y may depend on x).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The direct proof of the conditional proceeds by producing constructive witnesses for the existential claim given arbitrary instances of the hypothesis.

rubrics_metrics.name: Existence-and-uniqueness proof pattern
rubrics_metrics.description: To prove 'there exists a unique d such that P(d)', first produce an example d with P(d), then show any other d' with P(d') must equal d.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Two-part structure: existence (construct or exhibit) and uniqueness (prove any candidate equals the constructed one). Example: uniqueness of gcd with given linear-combination property.

rubrics_metrics.name: Constructive vs non-constructive proofs
rubrics_metrics.description: Constructive proofs explicitly exhibit an example; non-constructive proofs show that an example exists without actually giving it.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Text gives classical non-constructive example where one shows 'either x or y (one of two) is an irrational-to-irrational power that is rational' without specifying which, versus a constructive proof that explicitly gives x and y.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reduce rational fractions to lowest terms when assuming rationality
rubrics_metrics.description: When assuming a number is rational (as part of a contradiction), write it as a fraction 'in fully reduced form'; in particular note that numerator and denominator are not both even.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This reduction is used in irrationality proofs (e.g., √2) to deduce parity properties that lead to contradiction.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use division algorithm / smallest linear combination trick for gcd existence
rubrics_metrics.description: To prove gcd(a,b) can be written as ak + bℓ, consider A = {ax + by : x,y ∈ Z}, take its smallest positive element d, and show d divides a and b and equals gcd(a,b).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is a standard constructive technique (Bezout identity) that uses the division algorithm and minimality argument to establish existence of integer coefficients.

rubrics_metrics.name: Verification step in existence proofs
rubrics_metrics.description: Sometimes after presenting an example you must verify it actually satisfies the required property; omission makes the proof incomplete.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Text emphasizes that stating an example without showing how it works (e.g., that 1729 equals two different sums of cubes) would be incomplete; include the necessary arithmetic or reasoning.
